title: OpenAI Tools and Codex Agent Loops
summary: This intermediate-level module teaches you to structure, supervise, and evaluate a tool-using Codex workflow as a repeatable agent loop. After completing it, you can define boundaries, interpret tool results, decide whether another action is justified, and stop the loop safely.
objectives: Describe the roles of objectives, actions, observations, evaluation, and stopping conditions in a supervised agent loop.
Set explicit boundaries and success criteria before asking Codex to act.
Evaluate a tool result and decide whether to continue, revise the approach, or stop.
Distinguish a conceptual supervision model from unsupported claims about Codex implementation details.

sections.title: Source correction and scope
paragraphs: The cited source changed from the unverified local path content/modules/openai-practice/openai-tools-and-codex-agent-loops.json to the official OpenAI Codex repository listed in the sources field. This change affected the module's citation basis and the scope of its product claims.

The corrected module identifies Codex as an OpenAI coding agent, consistent with the official repository. Version-specific commands, configuration keys, and undocumented internal implementation details are omitted because the replaced citation did not establish them.
The loop presented below is a conceptual model for supervising tool-using work. It helps a learner reason about the interaction without claiming that it reproduces Codex's private internal process.

sections.title: Intermediate-level foundation
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes that you can describe a coding task, read ordinary command or file-operation results, and recognize whether an observed result matches an intended outcome. It does not assume knowledge of agent internals or provider configuration.

In this module, a tool is an externally executed capability that returns an observable result. An agent loop is a repeated workflow in which an objective guides an action, the action produces an observation, and that observation informs the next decision.

sections.title: Stages of a supervised agent loop
paragraphs: Start with an objective that states the desired outcome. Add boundaries that identify what may be changed, what must remain untouched, and what evidence will count as success. A vague objective makes later observations difficult to evaluate.

Next, let the agent select a bounded action. The action should advance the objective while remaining within the stated limits. Treat the returned output as an observation rather than as proof that the task is complete.

Evaluate the observation against the objective and boundaries. If it provides the required evidence and reveals no unresolved failure, stop successfully. If progress is possible but the approach needs adjustment, revise the next action. If a boundary would be crossed or safe progress is no longer possible, stop without continuing.

The resulting cycle is objective, bounded action, observation, evaluation, and either another action or a stop decision. Human supervision matters at the evaluation point because plausible output can still be incomplete, irrelevant, or inconsistent with the task.
sections.callout: A completed action is not the same as a completed objective. Stop only when the stated success evidence has been observed.

sections.title: Define boundaries before acting
paragraphs: A useful task statement names the target outcome, the permitted scope, the evidence required for completion, and conditions that require a pause. For example, a learner might permit inspection of relevant project material while requiring approval before any destructive or out-of-scope action.

Boundaries reduce ambiguity during evaluation. When an observation shows that the requested outcome would require work outside the permitted scope, the correct response is to pause and request a decision rather than silently expanding the task.

Success criteria should be observable. Replace a general instruction such as make it work with criteria that can be checked, such as preserving specified behavior and producing evidence that the requested correction is present.

sections.title: Evaluate observations and choose the next step
paragraphs: Classify each observation by asking three questions. Did the action produce evidence relevant to the objective? Did it remain within the boundaries? Does any failure or uncertainty remain unresolved?

Continue when the observation shows useful but incomplete progress and another bounded action can gather the missing evidence. Revise the approach when the action failed, addressed the wrong target, or produced ambiguous output. Stop when the success criteria are met, when a boundary blocks further work, or when continuing would repeat actions without adding evidence.

When an observation is unclear, do not convert uncertainty into a claim of success. Record what remains UNKNOWN and seek a bounded way to resolve it. If no supported way exists, stop and report the uncertainty.

sections.title: Trace a loop without assuming hidden internals
paragraphs: Consider a task to correct one documented behavior while leaving unrelated material unchanged. The objective is the specific correction, the boundary is the unchanged surrounding material, and the success evidence is a reviewable result showing only the required correction.

After the first action, inspect the observation. If it shows that unrelated material also changed, the loop should not declare success. The next decision should restore the boundary or pause if that cannot be done safely.

If the next observation shows the requested correction, no unrelated changes, and no unresolved failure, the success criteria are satisfied and the loop can stop. This reasoning is available from the visible task and observations, so it does not require access to hidden model reasoning or undocumented Codex internals.

questions.prompt: What should be established before the first action in the supervised loop described by this module?
choices: An objective, boundaries, and observable success criteria
A guarantee that every action will succeed
An undocumented account of the agent's internal process
Permission to expand the task whenever useful
questions.explanation: The module says to begin with an objective, boundaries, and evidence that will count as success.

questions.prompt: How should a returned tool result be treated?
choices: As automatic proof that the objective is complete
As an observation to evaluate against the objective and boundaries
As permission to ignore the original scope
As a reason to repeat the same action indefinitely
questions.explanation: A completed action produces an observation. The observation must still be evaluated before the loop continues or stops.

questions.prompt: What should happen when further progress would require crossing a stated boundary?
choices: The agent should silently widen the scope
The loop should report success immediately
The work should pause for a decision rather than crossing the boundary
The same action should be repeated without review
questions.explanation: The module instructs the learner to pause and request a decision when progress would require work outside the permitted scope.

questions.prompt: When is a successful stop justified?
choices: When the success criteria are met and no relevant failure remains unresolved
When the task description is vague
When an observation is still UNKNOWN
questions.explanation: The loop stops successfully only after observable evidence satisfies the stated criteria and no relevant unresolved failure remains.
